narrative:
The model estimated a 62.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that risk is above the threshold used for this decision, your law school application was denied; it is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but the admissions process treated it as too high to proceed.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. Your reported third-year decile was 3, compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students; this position pushed the prediction toward bar failure. The next most important factor was your first-year class standing: your second-decile position, versus an accepted average near 6.0, also pushed toward failure and reinforced concern about your academic preparation. Your LSAT score of 36 was the third most influential factor. Although it is slightly below the accepted average of about 37.2, its influence in this prediction was toward passing—it was a relative strength, not the reason for denial. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on the academic signals that drove the decision: meet with an academic advisor about your first- and third-year performance, ask what supports or remediation are available, and consider whether retaking the LSAT after structured preparation would strengthen your profile. If the school permits feedback or an appeal, request it, and consider applying when your record shows clearer evidence that you are ready for bar study.
